US.01.title: Homestead Act and Transcontinental Railroad
US.01.iCan: I can explain how the Homestead Act and the Transcontinental Railroad impacted the settlement of the West, including their effects on American Indians, immigrants, and settlers.
US.01.tnStandard: US.01 – Explain how the Homestead Act and the Transcontinental Railroad impacted the settlement of the West.

sections.heading: Sequence the expansion of the United States
sections.content: The Homestead Act of 1862 offered 160 acres of free land to settlers who would farm it for five years. Combined with the completion of the Transcontinental Railroad in 1869, these policies accelerated westward expansion as part of Manifest Destiny—the belief that Americans were destined to spread across the continent. The Union Pacific built westward from Omaha while the Central Pacific built eastward from Sacramento, meeting at Promontory Summit, Utah.

sections.heading: Impact on Western Settlement
sections.content: The Transcontinental Railroad dramatically reduced travel time from months to days, opening the West to settlement, commerce, and resource extraction. Towns sprang up along rail lines, and agricultural products could now reach eastern markets efficiently. However, this expansion came at tremendous cost to American Indian nations whose lands were taken and whose way of life was destroyed.

sections.heading: Impact on American Indians, Immigrants, and Settlers
sections.content: Western expansion devastated American Indian communities through forced relocations, broken treaties, and the near-extinction of buffalo herds they depended upon. Immigrants, particularly Chinese workers who built much of the Central Pacific, faced discrimination despite their crucial contributions. The "Buffalo Soldiers"—African American cavalry regiments—served on the frontier, including George Jordan of Williamson County, Tennessee, who received the Medal of Honor for his service.

vocab.def: An 1862 law that provided 160 acres of public land to settlers who agreed to live on and improve the land for five years, encouraging westward expansion.
vocab.simple: An 1862 law that provided 160 acres of public land to settlers who agreed to live on. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.

vocab.def: A continuous railroad line completed in 1869 that connected the eastern United States with the Pacific coast, revolutionizing transportation and commerce.
vocab.simple: A continuous railroad line completed in 1869 that connected the eastern United States with the Pacific coast. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.

vocab.def: The 19th-century movement of settlers, railroads, and U.S. authority across the continent toward the Pacific, encouraged by free land and new transportation.
The widely held 1800s belief that the United States was destined to expand across the entire continent, used to justify the displacement of American Indians.
A gift of public land from the government — to railroad companies or settlers — used to fund and accelerate western settlement.
An area of land set aside by the federal government for American Indian tribes, frequently far from their ancestral homelands.

US.02.title: Federal Policies Toward American Indians
US.02.iCan: I can examine federal policies toward American Indians, including the movement to reservations, assimilation, boarding schools, and the Dawes Act.
US.02.tnStandard: US.02 – Examine federal policies toward American Indians, including the movement to reservations, assimilation, boarding schools, and the Dawes Act.

sections.heading: Movement to Reservations
sections.content: After the Civil War, the federal government expanded a policy of confining American Indian nations to reservations—designated territories far smaller than their traditional homelands. Officials stated two goals: to open western land for white settlement and railroads, and to end armed conflict on the Plains. Many treaties were signed under military and economic pressure, and tribes surrendered millions of acres. Resistance continued: at the Battle of the Little Bighorn (1876), Lakota and Cheyenne forces under Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse defeated Lt. Col. George Custer—a Native victory that intensified U.S. efforts to break tribal power.

sections.heading: Assimilation and Boarding Schools
sections.content: Alongside removal, the government pursued a policy of assimilation—using schools and law to replace tribal cultures with Euro-American ones. At off-reservation boarding schools such as the Carlisle Indian Industrial School (founded 1879), Captain Richard H. Pratt summarized the aim in 1892: “Kill the Indian in him, and save the man.” Children were removed from their families and often forbidden to speak their languages, wear their clothing, or practice their religions. Historians today describe this systematic effort to erase Native identity as cultural genocide, and document its lasting, multi-generational harm.

sections.heading: The Dawes Act and Its Impact
sections.content: The Dawes Severalty Act of 1887 broke up communal tribal lands into individual allotments—160 acres to each head of a family—stating the goal of turning American Indians into independent farmers and U.S. citizens. The actual effect was a massive transfer of land: American Indians held about 150 million acres before the Act, and lost roughly two-thirds of their land base—over 90 million acres—by 1934. “Surplus” land was sold to white settlers, and additional allotted land was lost through taxation, fraud, and forced sales. The Act dismantled the communal landholding central to many tribal cultures.

vocab.def: Federal policy that confined Native American tribes to designated areas of land, often far from their ancestral territories, as part of efforts to control indigenous populations and open land for white settlement.
vocab.simple: Federal policy that confined Native American tribes to designated areas of land. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.

vocab.def: Federal policy aimed at forcing Native Americans to abandon their traditional cultures and adopt European-American ways of life, including language, religion, and customs.
vocab.simple: Federal policy aimed at forcing Native Americans to abandon their traditional cultures and adopt European-American ways of life. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.

vocab.def: An 1887 law that divided tribal lands into individual allotments for Native American families, aiming to break up reservations and assimilate Native Americans into mainstream American culture. It resulted in massive land loss.
vocab.simple: An 1887 law that divided tribal lands into individual allotments for Native American families. It changed land control and where Native communities could live.

vocab.def: The division of communal tribal land into small individual plots under the Dawes Act, which opened "surplus" land to white settlers and caused massive Native land loss.
Off-reservation schools, such as Carlisle, where Native children were forced to abandon their languages, names, and cultures to be "assimilated" into white society.
The right of a tribe or nation to govern itself; federal Indian policy in this era steadily eroded tribal sovereignty.

primarySources.context: In the late 19th century, the U.S. government pursued a policy of forced assimilation toward Native Americans, aiming to destroy tribal cultures and integrate Native people into white American society. A central feature of this policy was the Indian boarding school system, where children were taken from their families — often by force — and sent to government or church-run schools hundreds of miles away. At schools like the Carlisle Indian Industrial School in Pennsylvania, children were forbidden to speak their languages, required to wear Western clothing, given English names, and punished for practicing their cultures. The motto 'Kill the Indian, Save the Man' captured the brutal philosophy behind these institutions.

US.03.title: Compromise of 1877, Jim Crow & Plessy v. Ferguson
US.03.iCan: I can explain the impact of the Compromise of 1877, including Jim Crow laws, lynching, disenfranchisement methods, the efforts of Benjamin "Pap" Singleton and the Exodusters, and the Plessy v. Ferguson decision.
US.03.tnStandard: US.03 – Explain the impact of the Compromise of 1877, including Jim Crow laws, lynching, disenfranchisement methods, the efforts of Benjamin "Pap" Singleton and the Exodusters, and the Plessy v. Ferguson decision. (TCA)

sections.heading: The Election of 1876 and End of Reconstruction
sections.content: The disputed 1876 presidential election between Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel Tilden led to the Compromise of 1877. In exchange for the presidency, Hayes agreed to withdraw federal troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction. This abandonment left African Americans without federal protection against increasingly hostile state governments.

sections.heading: Jim Crow Laws, Lynching, and Disenfranchisement
sections.content: With federal protection gone, Southern states implemented Jim Crow laws enforcing racial segregation in all aspects of life. African Americans faced systematic disenfranchisement through poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and white primaries. Those who resisted faced terrorism, including lynching—public murders that went unpunished and were often celebrated by white communities.

sections.heading: Pap Singleton and the Exodusters
sections.content: Benjamin "Pap" Singleton, a formerly enslaved man, organized the migration of thousands of African Americans from the South to Kansas in 1879. These "Exodusters" sought to escape violence and oppression, establishing communities like Nicodemus, Kansas. While conditions in Kansas were often harsh, the Exoduster movement represented African American agency and resistance to Jim Crow terror.

sections.heading: Plessy v. Ferguson and "Separate But Equal"
sections.content: The 1896 Supreme Court decision in Plessy v. Ferguson established the "separate but equal" doctrine, ruling that racial segregation was constitutional as long as facilities were supposedly equal. In practice, facilities for African Americans were grossly inferior. This decision legitimized Jim Crow segregation for nearly sixty years until Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

vocab.def: An informal agreement that resolved the disputed 1876 presidential election, resulting in Rutherford B. Hayes becoming president in exchange for removing federal troops from the South, effectively ending Reconstruction.
vocab.simple: An informal agreement that resolved the disputed 1876 presidential election. It changed who held power after major conflicts.

vocab.def: State and local laws enacted primarily in the Southern states between 1877 and the 1960s that enforced racial segregation and denied African Americans their constitutional rights.
vocab.simple: State and local laws enacted primarily in the Southern states between 1877 and the 1960s that enforced racial. It shaped racial rules and unequal treatment in daily life.

vocab.def: The systematic denial of voting rights through methods such as poll taxes, literacy tests, grandfather clauses, and violence, primarily targeting African American voters.
vocab.simple: The systematic taking away of voting rights through methods such as poll taxes. It changed who could vote and who had political power.

vocab.def: An 1896 Supreme Court decision that upheld racial segregation under the doctrine of "separate but equal," legitimizing Jim Crow laws for nearly 60 years.
vocab.simple: An 1896 Supreme Court decision that upheld racial separation by race under the doctrine of "separate but equal,". It shaped racial rules and unequal treatment in daily life.

vocab.def: African Americans who migrated from the South to Kansas and other western states in the late 1870s, seeking to escape racial violence and economic oppression. Led by figures like Benjamin "Pap" Singleton.
vocab.simple: African Americans who moved from the South to Kansas and other western states in the late 1870s. It shaped racial rules and unequal treatment in daily life.

bios.name: Ida B. Wells
accomplish: Led the first anti-lynching campaign in American history
Co-founded the NAACP
Documented over 700 lynchings in "Southern Horrors"
Organized African American women for suffrage
Challenged segregation in courts and direct action
bios.legacy: Ida B. Wells was a fearless journalist who exposed the truth about lynching in the American South when no one else would. After a white mob murdered three of her friends in Memphis, she launched a crusade that documented the real reasons behind racial violence—economic competition and white supremacy—rather than the false claims used to justify it. Her investigative journalism challenged both Southern violence and Northern indifference. Wells also fought for women's suffrage and was among the founders of the NAACP, though she was often marginalized for her uncompromising stance.

bios.name: Booker T. Washington
accomplish: Founded and led Tuskegee Institute
Became the most influential African American leader of his era
Delivered the "Atlanta Compromise" speech
Advised Presidents Roosevelt and Taft on race relations
Published "Up from Slavery," an influential autobiography
bios.legacy: Booker T. Washington was the most prominent African American leader from 1895 until his death in 1915. Born into slavery, he built Tuskegee Institute into the leading black educational institution in America. His "Atlanta Compromise" speech advocated industrial education and economic self-improvement while temporarily accepting political and social inequality. This approach won white support and significant funding but was criticized by W.E.B. Du Bois and others who demanded full civil and political rights. The debate between Washington and Du Bois shaped African American political thought for generations.

primarySources.title: Plessy v. Ferguson Decision
primarySources.author: Supreme Court of the United States
primarySources.excerpt: Laws permitting, and even requiring, their separation in places where they are liable to be brought into contact do not necessarily imply the inferiority of either race to the other... We consider the underlying fallacy of the plaintiff's argument to consist in the assumption that the enforced separation of the two races stamps the colored race with a badge of inferiority.

citation.apaCitation: Supreme Court of the United States. (1896). Plessy v. Ferguson, 163 U.S. 537. Library of Congress. https://www.loc.gov/item/usrep163537/

primarySources.context: After the Compromise of 1877 ended Reconstruction, Southern states systematically dismantled the civil and political rights that African Americans had gained after the Civil War. By the 1890s, a system of racial segregation laws — known as Jim Crow — had spread across the South, enforced by violence, poll taxes, literacy tests, and legal barriers. The 1896 Supreme Court case Plessy v. Ferguson arose when Homer Plessy, a man of mixed race, deliberately challenged a Louisiana law requiring separate railroad cars. The Court's 7-1 ruling created the 'separate but equal' doctrine, providing legal cover for segregation for the next 58 years until Brown v. Board of Education (1954).

options.text: That state-enforced separation itself signals and enforces inequality, regardless of facility quality.
That segregation was acceptable as long as both facilities were physically identical.
That the Constitution explicitly required racial separation.
That African Americans had freely chosen separate facilities.

primarySources.explanation: DOK 3: This requires evaluating the Court’s logic. Justice Harlan’s dissent — and later Brown v. Board (1954) — argued that government-mandated separation is inherently unequal because the law itself brands a group as inferior, directly rejecting the "separate but equal" reasoning.

primarySources.excerpt: My people, for the want of land—we needed land for our children—and their disadvantages that caused my heart to grieve and sorrow; pity for my race, sir, that was coming down, instead of going up—that caused me to go to work for them. Right emphatically, I tell you today, I woke them up; and I have sent out perhaps seventy thousand to ninety thousand.

primarySources.context: After the Civil War, the brief hope of Reconstruction — where freedpeople gained political rights, owned land, and held elected office — was crushed by the Compromise of 1877 and the rise of racial terror in the South. Faced with violence, sharecropping, and the systematic denial of rights, many African Americans sought new lives elsewhere. Benjamin 'Pap' Singleton, a formerly enslaved man from Tennessee, became one of the most important organizers of the Exoduster movement, convincing tens of thousands of Black Southerners to migrate to Kansas between 1877 and 1880, where they could own land and escape the worst of Southern oppression.

US.04.title: Gilded Age Politics and Economics
US.04.iCan: I can analyze the causes and consequences of Gilded Age politics and economics, including political machines, major scandals, civil service reform, and economic differences between farmers, wage earners, and industrial capitalists.
US.04.tnStandard: US.04 – Analyze the causes and consequences of Gilded Age politics and economics as well as the significance of the rise of political machines, major scandals, civil service reform, and the economic difference between farmers, wage earners, and industrial capitalists, including: Boss Tweed, Thomas Nast, Credit Mobilier, Spoils system and President James A. Garfield's assassination, Pendleton Act, Interstate Commerce Act.

sections.heading: Political Machines and Boss Tweed
sections.content: The Gilded Age (1870s-1900) saw the rise of powerful political machines that controlled city governments through patronage and corruption. Boss Tweed's Tammany Hall in New York City epitomized this system, funneling millions in public funds to Tweed and his associates. Political cartoonist Thomas Nast exposed Tweed's corruption through devastating illustrations in Harper's Weekly.

sections.heading: Major Scandals and the Spoils System
sections.content: The era was marked by corruption at all levels. The Crédit Mobilier scandal revealed that railroad executives and congressmen had profited enormously from fraudulent construction contracts. The spoils system—giving government jobs to political supporters regardless of qualification—reached its peak. President James Garfield's assassination by a disappointed office-seeker in 1881 finally prompted reform.

sections.heading: Civil Service Reform
sections.content: Garfield's assassination led to the Pendleton Civil Service Act of 1883, which established merit-based hiring for federal positions through competitive examinations. This began the long process of professionalizing government service, though political influence remained significant in many positions.

sections.heading: Economic Disparity
sections.content: The Gilded Age saw extreme wealth concentration among industrial capitalists while farmers struggled with falling crop prices, high railroad shipping rates, and debt. Wage earners faced dangerous working conditions, long hours, and low pay. The Interstate Commerce Act of 1887 attempted to regulate railroad rates, representing early federal intervention in the economy.

vocab.def: The period from roughly 1870 to 1900 characterized by rapid economic growth, industrialization, and extreme wealth inequality. Named by Mark Twain to suggest that a thin layer of prosperity covered deep social problems.
vocab.simple: The period from roughly 1870 to 1900 characterized by rapid economic growth. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

vocab.def: Corrupt organizations that controlled city politics through patronage, bribery, and vote manipulation, often providing services to immigrants in exchange for political support.
vocab.simple: Corrupt organizations that controlled city politics through patronage. It changed who could vote and who had political power.

vocab.def: The practice of rewarding political supporters with government jobs regardless of qualifications, based on the principle "to the victor belong the spoils."
vocab.simple: The practice of rewarding political supporters with government jobs regardless of qualifications. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

vocab.def: William M. Tweed, leader of New York City's Tammany Hall political machine, who controlled city politics and stole millions through kickbacks and corruption in the 1860s-1870s.
vocab.simple: He led New York City's Tammany Hall machine and used bribery to control city politics. His group stole millions of dollars from taxpayers through corrupt contracts.

vocab.def: A political cartoonist whose illustrations exposed Boss Tweed's corruption and helped bring down the Tammany Hall machine, demonstrating the power of the press.
vocab.simple: A political cartoonist whose illustrations exposed Boss Tweed's corruption and helped bring down the Tammany Hall machine. It changed daily life, rights, or power during this era.

vocab.def: An 1883 federal law that established the Civil Service Commission and required government jobs to be awarded based on merit through competitive examinations rather than political connections.
vocab.simple: An 1883 federal law that established the Civil Service Commission and required government jobs to be awarded based. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

primarySources.title: Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act
primarySources.author: U.S. Congress
primarySources.excerpt: No person in the public service is for that reason under any obligations to contribute to any political fund, or to render any political service, and he will not be removed or otherwise prejudiced for refusing to do so... No person in said service has any right to use his official authority or influence to coerce the political action of any person or body.
primarySources.question: What problem was the Pendleton Act designed to address?

citation.mlaCitation: United States Congress. "Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act." 1883. National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/pendleton-act.
citation.apaCitation: United States Congress. (1883). Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act. National Archives. https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/pendleton-act

primarySources.context: During the Gilded Age, the 'spoils system' — where elected officials rewarded political supporters with government jobs regardless of qualifications — had corrupted American government at every level. Political machines like Tammany Hall in New York City handed out thousands of jobs to loyal party members, and government workers were expected to donate a portion of their salaries to political campaigns. The assassination of President James Garfield in 1881 by a disappointed office-seeker shocked the nation and created overwhelming pressure for reform. The Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act of 1883 created a merit-based civil service system, requiring competitive exams for federal jobs and prohibiting political coercion of government workers.

British observer James Bryce documented how these bosses worked. Reformers responded with the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act (1883), which created merit-based federal hiring. Reading Bryce's description alongside the reform law shows the problem and the solution side by side.

US.05.title: Inventions & Innovations of Business Leaders & Entrepreneurs
US.05.iCan: I can describe the changes in American life that resulted from the inventions and innovations of business leaders and entrepreneurs of the period, including Alexander Graham Bell, Andrew Carnegie, Thomas Edison, John D. Rockefeller, Madam C.J. Walker, and George Washington Carver.
US.05.tnStandard: US.05 – Describe the changes in American life that resulted from the inventions and innovations of business leaders and entrepreneurs of the period, including: Alexander Graham Bell, Henry Bessemer, Andrew Carnegie, Thomas Edison, J.P. Morgan, John D. Rockefeller, Nikola Tesla, Cornelius Vanderbilt, Madam C.J. Walker, George Washington Carver.

sections.heading: Technological Innovations
sections.content: The late 19th century saw transformative inventions that reshaped American life. Alexander Graham Bell's telephone (1876) revolutionized communication. Thomas Edison's electrical systems and light bulb brought power to homes and factories. Nikola Tesla's alternating current system enabled long-distance electrical transmission. Henry Bessemer's steel process made skyscrapers and modern infrastructure possible.

sections.heading: Industrial Titans
sections.content: Andrew Carnegie built a steel empire through vertical integration, controlling every step from iron mines to finished products. John D. Rockefeller's Standard Oil pioneered horizontal integration, buying out competitors to dominate the oil industry. J.P. Morgan wielded enormous financial power, reorganizing railroads and creating U.S. Steel. Cornelius Vanderbilt consolidated railroad networks, enabling national commerce.

sections.heading: African American Entrepreneurs
sections.content: Despite facing discrimination, African American entrepreneurs made significant contributions. Madam C.J. Walker became America's first female self-made millionaire through her hair care products, employing thousands of Black women. George Washington Carver's agricultural research at Tuskegee Institute developed hundreds of products from peanuts and sweet potatoes, helping diversify Southern agriculture.

vocab.def: Wealthy industrialists of the late 1800s who built massive business empires. Critics called them "robber barons" for ruthless practices; supporters called them "captains of industry" for economic growth.
vocab.simple: Wealthy industrialists of the late 1800s who built massive business empires. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

vocab.def: A business strategy where a company controls all stages of production, from raw materials to finished product, as practiced by Andrew Carnegie in the steel industry.
vocab.simple: A business strategy where a company controls all stages of production. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

vocab.def: A business strategy where a company buys out competitors in the same industry to reduce competition and control prices, as practiced by John D. Rockefeller in oil.
vocab.simple: A business strategy where a company buys out competitors in the same industry to reduce competition and control. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

vocab.def: Complete control of a product or service by a single company, eliminating competition and allowing the company to set prices.
vocab.simple: Complete control of a product or service by a single company. It changed how money and power were controlled in the economy.

vocab.def: A legal arrangement where stockholders in several companies transferred their shares to a single board of trustees, creating a monopoly while appearing to remain separate companies.
vocab.simple: A legal arrangement where stockholders in several companies transferred their shares to a board of trustees. It changed how money and power were controlled in the economy.

vocab.def: An efficient method of making steel by blowing air through molten iron, developed by Henry Bessemer, that made mass production of steel possible and revolutionized construction and manufacturing.
vocab.simple: An efficient method of making steel by blowing air through molten iron. It changed rights and rules that people had to live under.

bios.name: Andrew Carnegie
accomplish: Built Carnegie Steel Company into the largest steel producer in the world
Pioneered vertical integration in American industry
Donated over $350 million to charitable causes
Funded construction of over 2,500 public libraries
Established Carnegie Hall, Carnegie Mellon University, and the Carnegie Foundation
bios.legacy: Andrew Carnegie embodied both the promise and contradictions of the Gilded Age. Rising from immigrant poverty to become one of the richest Americans in history, he revolutionized the steel industry and helped transform the United States into an industrial powerhouse. His "Gospel of Wealth" philosophy argued that the rich had a moral obligation to distribute their fortunes for the public good, establishing the modern concept of philanthropy. Yet his legacy is complicated by the Homestead Strike of 1892, where workers were killed in a violent confrontation with Pinkerton guards.

bios.name: John D. Rockefeller
accomplish: Founded Standard Oil, controlling 90% of U.S. oil refining
Pioneered the trust as a form of business organization
Became the first American worth over $1 billion
Established the Rockefeller Foundation
Founded the University of Chicago
bios.legacy: John D. Rockefeller transformed the American oil industry and created the model for modern corporate monopolies. His Standard Oil Trust became so powerful that it sparked the antitrust movement and the Sherman Antitrust Act of 1890. Through ruthless business practices including secret rebates from railroads and predatory pricing, he eliminated competitors and controlled nearly all American oil refining. In later life, he became one of history's greatest philanthropists, donating over $500 million to medical research, education, and scientific advancement.

bios.name: Thomas Edison
accomplish: Invented the practical incandescent light bulb
Created the first industrial research laboratory
Developed the phonograph
Invented the motion picture camera
Held 1,093 U.S. patents
bios.legacy: Thomas Edison was the most prolific inventor in American history and helped create the modern world of electric light, recorded sound, and motion pictures. His greatest innovation may have been the industrial research laboratory itself—a systematic approach to invention that transformed technology development. Edison's work electrifying cities changed daily life, extended productive hours, and created new industries. His rivalry with Nikola Tesla over AC versus DC power distribution shaped the electrical infrastructure we use today.

bios.name: Cornelius Vanderbilt
accomplish: Built the largest fortune in American history to that time
Created the New York Central Railroad system
Pioneered steamship travel across the Atlantic
Established Grand Central Depot in New York City
Donated $1 million to found Vanderbilt University
bios.legacy: Cornelius Vanderbilt was America's first great transportation magnate, building empires first in steamships and then in railroads. His ruthless business tactics—including rate wars, stock manipulation, and bribery—established patterns that later industrialists would follow. The New York Central Railroad he created connected the Midwest to the East Coast and helped make New York City the nation's commercial capital. At his death, his fortune of $100 million was the largest ever accumulated by an American.

bios.name: J.P. Morgan
accomplish: Created J.P. Morgan & Co., the most powerful bank in America
Organized U.S. Steel, the first billion-dollar corporation
Bailed out the U.S. government during the Panic of 1893
Reorganized and consolidated major railroads
Amassed one of the world's greatest art collections
bios.legacy: J.P. Morgan was the most powerful private banker in American history, wielding influence over the nation's finances that rivaled the government itself. His ability to organize massive corporate consolidations and rescue the economy during financial panics made him indispensable—and feared. Morgan's dominance led directly to the creation of the Federal Reserve System in 1913, designed to prevent any private individual from ever again holding such power over American finance.

primarySources.title: The Gospel of Wealth

primarySources.question: A wealthy 1890s steel magnate funds free public libraries across the country instead of leaving his entire fortune to his heirs. Whose philosophy does this best reflect, and why?

primarySources.context: Andrew Carnegie was the most famous example of a 'rags to riches' story in Gilded Age America. An immigrant from Scotland who started as a factory bobbin boy, Carnegie built the largest steel company in the world through relentless efficiency, brutal labor practices, and shrewd business dealings. By the late 1880s, he was worth hundreds of millions of dollars. In 'The Gospel of Wealth' (1889), Carnegie argued that wealthy men had a duty to use their fortunes to benefit society — a philosophy that justified both extreme wealth concentration and a paternalistic approach to charity. Carnegie himself donated over $350 million to libraries, universities, and public institutions before his death.

The opposite of Carnegie’s view, because he insisted fortunes pass to children.
The opposite of Carnegie’s view, because he opposed all charitable giving.

primarySources.explanation: DOK 2: Students apply the source to a new case. Carnegie argued the rich should live modestly and administer surplus wealth "as trust funds" for the public good — funding libraries is a textbook example of his Gospel of Wealth.

primarySources.context: Madam C.J. Walker (born Sarah Breedlove) became the first self-made female millionaire in American history at a time when both race and gender severely limited economic opportunities. Born to formerly enslaved parents in 1867, she developed a line of hair care products for African American women and built a national sales network of Black female agents. Walker's success was celebrated in the Black press as proof that African Americans could achieve economic independence in spite of Jim Crow laws and racial discrimination. The Indianapolis Freeman, an important Black newspaper, covered Walker's story as an inspiration to its readers.

US.06.title: Industrial Centers and Urbanization
US.06.iCan: I can locate major industrial centers and describe how industrialization influenced the movement of people from rural to urban areas.
US.06.tnStandard: US.06 – Locate the following major industrial centers, and describe how industrialization influenced the movement of people from rural to urban areas: Boston, Chicago, New York City, Pittsburgh, San Francisco.

sections.heading: Major Industrial Centers
sections.content: Industrialization concentrated in cities with geographic advantages. Pittsburgh became the steel capital due to access to coal, iron ore, and rivers. Chicago emerged as a railroad hub and meatpacking center. New York City dominated finance and trade through its port. Boston led in textiles and manufacturing. San Francisco served as the gateway to Pacific trade and western resources.

sections.heading: Rural-to-Urban Migration
sections.content: Industrialization drew millions from farms to cities seeking factory jobs. The promise of wages attracted both native-born Americans and immigrants. Cities grew explosively—Chicago's population increased from 30,000 in 1850 to over 1 million by 1890. This rapid growth created overcrowded tenements, inadequate sanitation, and new social challenges.

sections.heading: Geographic Factors in Industrial Location
sections.content: Industries located based on access to raw materials, transportation, markets, and labor. Steel mills clustered near coal and iron deposits. Textile mills used water power and later concentrated near ports for cotton imports. Meatpacking centered in Chicago due to railroad connections to cattle ranges and eastern markets. These patterns shaped regional development for generations.

vocab.def: The rapid growth of cities due to industrialization and mass migration, transforming America from a predominantly rural to urban society.
vocab.simple: The rapid growth of cities due to factory growth and mass moving. It changed where people lived and worked in growing cities.

vocab.def: A farmers' organization founded in 1867 that advocated for railroad regulation and fought against monopolistic practices that harmed farmers through high shipping rates.
vocab.simple: A farmers' organization formed in the 1860s-1870s to combat the power of railroads and grain elevator companies. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.

vocab.def: A political movement in the 1890s representing farmers and workers who sought government regulation of railroads, graduated income tax, and the free coinage of silver to combat economic inequality.
vocab.simple: A political movement representing the interests of ordinary people. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.

vocab.def: An 1887 federal law that created the Interstate Commerce Commission to regulate railroad rates and practices, representing the first federal regulatory agency.
vocab.simple: An 1887 federal law that created the Interstate Trade Commission to regulate railroad rates and practices. It changed travel, trade, and how far-away places were connected.

vocab.def: A crowded, often unsafe urban apartment building where many poor and immigrant families lived during rapid industrial-era city growth.
The shift from an economy based on farming and handcraft to one based on large factories, machines, and mass production.

bios.name: Samuel Gompers
accomplish: Founded the American Federation of Labor (AFL)
Served as AFL President for 37 years
Pioneered "bread and butter" unionism focusing on wages and hours
Advocated for the 8-hour workday
Testified before Congress on labor conditions
bios.legacy: Samuel Gompers built the American Federation of Labor into the most successful labor organization in American history. His strategy of "pure and simple" unionism—focusing on immediate economic gains rather than radical political change—helped establish collective bargaining as an accepted part of American industrial relations. By organizing skilled workers by craft and avoiding socialist politics, Gompers made the labor movement respectable to mainstream America, though critics argued this approach excluded unskilled workers and minorities.

bios.name: Eugene V. Debs
accomplish: Founded the American Railway Union
Led the Pullman Strike of 1894
Co-founded the Industrial Workers of the World (IWW)
Five-time Socialist Party presidential candidate
Received nearly 1 million votes for president in 1920 while imprisoned
bios.legacy: Eugene V. Debs was the most influential socialist in American history. His transformation from railroad union leader to socialist presidential candidate represented the radical wing of the labor movement that challenged industrial capitalism itself. The Pullman Strike he led in 1894 demonstrated both the power of industrial unionism and the willingness of the federal government to use military force against workers. His imprisonment for opposing World War I made him a martyr for free speech and working-class solidarity.

primarySources.title: How the Other Half Lives
primarySources.author: Jacob Riis
primarySources.excerpt: In the tenements all the influences make for evil; because they are the hot-beds of the epidemics that carry death to rich and poor alike; the nurseries of pauperism and crime that fill our jails and police courts; that throw off a scum of forty thousand human wrecks to the island asylums and workhouses year by year.
primarySources.question: How does Jacob Riis characterize living conditions in tenements?

citation.mlaCitation: Riis, Jacob. "How the Other Half Lives." 1890. Library of Congress, www.loc.gov/item/71184754/.
citation.apaCitation: Riis, J. (1890). How the other half lives. Library of Congress. https://www.loc.gov/item/71184754/

primarySources.context: By 1890, millions of immigrants — primarily from Southern and Eastern Europe — had poured into American cities to work in factories, mines, and mills. In cities like New York, Chicago, and Pittsburgh, the poor were crowded into tenement buildings: dark, airless apartment buildings with shared toilets, no running water, and extreme overcrowding. Jacob Riis, a Danish immigrant himself who had experienced poverty firsthand, used the new technology of flash photography to document conditions in New York's Lower East Side slums. 'How the Other Half Lives' shocked middle-class readers and helped spark the progressive reform movement.

primarySources.context: Between 1880 and 1920, over 20 million immigrants arrived in the United States — the largest wave of immigration in American history. Many came from Italy, Poland, Russia, and other parts of Southern and Eastern Europe, drawn by the promise of economic opportunity and fleeing poverty, violence, and persecution. The reality of American life often differed sharply from the dream: immigrants were crowded into urban tenements, took the hardest and lowest-paying factory jobs, and faced widespread discrimination. This folk saying — widely circulated among Italian immigrants — captured the bitter gap between immigrant expectations and the reality of life in industrial America.

US.07.title: Immigration: Old vs. New Immigrants
US.07.iCan: I can describe the differences between "old" and "new" immigrants; explain entry points (Ellis Island and Angel Island), push and pull factors, and the formation of ethnic clusters; and analyze nativism and restrictions such as the Chinese Exclusion Act and the Gentlemen’s Agreement on American society.
US.07.tnStandard: US.07 – Describe the differences between "old" and "new" immigrants, analyze the assimilation process for "new" immigrants, and determine the impacts of increased migration on American society, including: Angel Island, Ellis Island, Push and pull factors, Ethnic clusters, Jane Addams, Competition for jobs, Rise of nativism, Jacob Riis, Chinese Exclusion Act and Gentleman's Agreement.

sections.heading: Old and New Immigrants
sections.content: "Old" immigrants (pre-1880) came primarily from Northern and Western Europe—Britain, Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia. They often spoke English or related languages and were predominantly Protestant. "New" immigrants (1880-1920) came from Southern and Eastern Europe—Italy, Poland, Russia, Greece—as well as Asia. They brought different languages, religions (Catholic, Orthodox, Jewish), and customs that many Americans viewed with suspicion.

sections.heading: Entry Points and the Assimilation Process
sections.content: Ellis Island in New York Harbor processed millions of European immigrants, while Angel Island in San Francisco served Asian immigrants with far more restrictive procedures. New immigrants faced difficult assimilation: language barriers, discrimination, and unfamiliar customs. Jane Addams's Hull House in Chicago pioneered settlement houses that helped immigrants learn English, navigate American systems, and maintain cultural connections.

sections.heading: Push and Pull Factors
sections.content: Push factors drove people from their homelands: religious persecution (especially of Jews in Russia), poverty, political upheaval, and lack of opportunity. Pull factors attracted them to America: economic opportunity, religious freedom, land availability, and established immigrant communities. Letters from successful immigrants encouraged others to follow.

sections.heading: Nativism and Restriction
sections.content: The rise of nativism—hostility toward immigrants—led to restrictive legislation. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 banned Chinese immigration for ten years (repeatedly renewed until 1943). The Gentleman's Agreement of 1907 limited Japanese immigration. Jacob Riis's photographs and writings, including "How the Other Half Lives," exposed immigrant living conditions, prompting both sympathy and nativist fears.

vocab.def: Immigrants who came to the United States primarily from Northern and Western Europe (England, Ireland, Germany, Scandinavia) before 1880, often Protestant and more easily assimilated.
vocab.simple: Immigrants who came to the United States primarily from Northern and Western Europe (England. It changed who could enter the United States and how newcomers were treated.

vocab.def: Immigrants who came to the United States primarily from Southern and Eastern Europe (Italy, Poland, Russia) and Asia after 1880, often Catholic, Jewish, or Orthodox Christian, facing greater discrimination.

vocab.simple: The primary immigration processing station in New York Harbor from 1892 to 1954. It changed who could enter the United States and how newcomers were treated.

vocab.simple: The immigration station in San Francisco Bay from 1910 to 1940 that primarily processed Asian immigrants. It changed who could enter the United States and how newcomers were treated.

bios.name: Jane Addams
accomplish: Co-founded Hull House, the most influential settlement house in America
First American woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize (1931)
Founded the Women's International League for Peace and Freedom
Pioneered the profession of social work
Advocated for child labor laws, women's suffrage, and immigrant rights
bios.legacy: Jane Addams pioneered the settlement house movement and helped create the profession of social work. Hull House became a model for social reform, offering education, childcare, and cultural programs to Chicago's immigrant communities. Addams connected local reform to broader movements for labor rights, women's suffrage, and international peace. Her work demonstrated that addressing poverty required understanding immigrant communities on their own terms and challenging the economic system that created inequality.

primarySources.title: Chinese Exclusion Act
primarySources.author: U.S. Congress
primarySources.excerpt: The coming of Chinese laborers to this country endangers the good order of certain localities within the territory thereof: Therefore... the coming of Chinese laborers to the United States be, and the same is hereby, suspended; and during such suspension it shall not be lawful for any Chinese laborer to come, or having so come after the expiration of said ninety days, to remain within the United States.
primarySources.question: What was the stated justification for the Chinese Exclusion Act?

citation.mlaCitation: United States Congress. "Chinese Exclusion Act." 1882. National Archives, https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/chinese-exclusion-act.
citation.apaCitation: United States Congress. (1882). Chinese Exclusion Act. National Archives. https://www.archives.gov/milestone-documents/chinese-exclusion-act

primarySources.context: Chinese immigrants had played an essential role in building the transcontinental railroad and developing the American West, yet they faced intense racial hostility from white workers and politicians. Anti-Chinese riots broke out in cities across the West, and nativist groups pressured Congress to restrict Chinese immigration. The Chinese Exclusion Act of 1882 was the first major federal law to restrict immigration based on race and nationality, banning Chinese laborers from entering the country and barring Chinese immigrants from ever becoming U.S. citizens. It would not be fully repealed until 1943.

primarySources.explanation: The Act claims "The coming of Chinese laborers to this country endangers the good order of certain localities," using this as justification for exclusion.

primarySources.title: Twenty Years at Hull-House
primarySources.author: Jane Addams
primarySources.excerpt: Hull-House was soberly opened on the theory that the dependence of classes on each other is reciprocal... We were ready to perform the humblest neighborhood services. We were asked to wash the newborn babies, and to prepare the dead for burial, to nurse the sick, and to "mind the children."
primarySources.question: According to Jane Addams, what was the philosophy behind Hull-House?

citation.mlaCitation: Addams, Jane. "Twenty Years at Hull-House." 1910. University of Pennsylvania Digital Library, digital.library.upenn.edu/women/addams/hullhouse/hullhouse.html.
citation.apaCitation: Addams, J. (1910). Twenty years at Hull-House. University of Pennsylvania Digital Library. https://digital.library.upenn.edu/women/addams/hullhouse/hullhouse.html

primarySources.context: Jane Addams and Ellen Gates Starr founded Hull-House in Chicago in 1889 in the heart of a crowded immigrant neighborhood. Hull-House became the most famous settlement house in America — a community center where college-educated reformers lived alongside recent immigrants and offered services including English classes, childcare, job training, and cultural programs. Addams believed that by actually living in the community, reformers could learn from immigrant neighbors rather than simply helping them from a distance. Hull-House became a center of Progressive Era reform, and Addams went on to win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1931.
